activities.text: You will leave Djerba on the Ajim ferry, which crosses a channel about 2.5 km wide to El Jorf on the mainland. Before boarding, explore Ajim, a major fishing port once known for its sponges. Its alleys served as the setting for Mos Eisley, the port city in the first Star Wars movie. The facade of the cantina, the bar in the movie, is a former bakery. In summer and during vacation periods, ferry wait times can be long.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Tunisia in 9 Days: Djerba, Ksour, the Sahara, and Oases

visits.text: Colorful boats, fishermen sorting fish on the quay, and white houses all around: Bizerte’s old harbor is best explored slowly, on foot. A canal, first dug in Phoenician times, links it to the main harbor. To the north, the kasbah, or citadel, retains ramparts you can climb to see the boats from above. The neighboring main harbor served as a French naval base until October 15, 1963, seven years after Tunisia’s independence. Come in the morning, when the fishermen unload their catch.

Between 1570 and 1573, the Ottomans built the Spanish Fort on the hill overlooking Bizerte’s medina to defend it against Spanish attacks. Its terrace, about 40 m above sea level, offers the broadest view of the white rooftops, harbor channel, and Lake Bizerte. In summer, the fort becomes an open-air theater for the Bizerte International Festival. Head up at the end of your visit before taking the road south.

Between Bizerte’s souks and old harbor, Rebaa Mosque is recognizable by its Ottoman-style octagonal, or eight-sided, minaret. It dates from the 17th century and remains open only to worshippers. Right next door, the fish market comes alive early in the morning. Farther on, the Andalusian Quarter was built by Muslims expelled from Spain. Look for its grilles and blue-painted doors, and photograph the facades rather than the residents.

activities.text: If the sky is clear, continue to Cape Angela, about 15 km from Bizerte. This rocky headland, marked by a stone monument, is presented as the northernmost point of the African continent. No shuttle goes there: drive and allow 1 hour for the round trip, including the stop.

days_plan.itin_title: Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem

visits.text: A single re-erected column, 12.5 m tall, is enough to convey the scale of the Antonine Baths in Carthage. These public baths, built between 145 and 162 beside the sea, are the largest Roman baths built in Africa. Mostly the underground levels survive, but the now-vanished vaults rose more than 29 m. Buy the Carthage combination ticket here for 12 dinars; it also covers the Roman villas, theater, and La Malga Cisterns. Do not photograph the neighboring presidential palace.

Carthage’s most pleasant district is the Roman Villas Park, on Odeon Hill. In the 2nd century, wealthy families built houses here with mosaic and marble floors, such as the Villa of the Aviary. Look for the mosaic that imitates a tigress’s hide, rendered in color against a white background. The nearby odeon, a small performance hall, hosted concerts and literary competitions. The same combination ticket admits you to the Roman theater close by.

In 146 BC, the Romans launched their final assault on Carthage from the Punic, or Carthaginian, ports. Their shape is still visible in the landscape: a round lagoon, the former military harbor, connected to a rectangular lagoon, the former commercial harbor. The ancient author Appian describes shelters for 220 warships. Archaeologists have found space for around 160 to 170 boats. Start with the small museum on the central islet: its models show the harbor at different periods.

A peaceful garden today, the Tophet of Salammbô remains a much-debated site in Carthage. This Punic sanctuary, dedicated to the deities Tanit and Baal Hammon, has yielded around 20,000 urns containing the burned bones of very young children. Ancient Greek and Roman authors accused Carthage of sacrificing children. Some present-day researchers instead interpret the site as a cemetery for newborns and children who died very young. The debate remains unresolved. Allow 40 minutes, combining your visit with a walk to the nearby Punic ports.

If you wonder how an ancient city obtained its water, head up to the La Malga Cisterns in Carthage. These fifteen reservoirs, built under Emperor Hadrian, could store around 60,000 m³. This was the endpoint of the aqueduct from Zaghouan, whose source you will see later in the trip. Until the 20th century, families even lived in some of the cisterns, which were converted into homes, stables, or storage spaces. The combination ticket includes them, along with the Roman amphitheater.

Finish at the Early Christian Museum of Carthage, which reopened in December 2025 after renovation. “Early Christian” refers to the earliest days of Christianity. Within its grounds, you will see the remains of a basilica and a stretch of Roman road, with brand-new signage. Good to know: admission to Carthage’s sites is free on the first Sunday of each month.

days_plan.itin_title: Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem

places.name: Chenini

visits.text: Our favorite stop on the route is Chenini, a Berber village clinging to a ridge between two peaks at an elevation of about 500 m. At the very top, the ksar is a fortified granary where harvests were kept safe from raiders. Its oldest sections date to the 12th century. Below it, homes are carved into the rock, some of them still inhabited. Follow the path up to the ksar and stay until sunset, when the peaks turn golden.

Locals tell of seven young men, persecuted for their faith, who fell asleep in a cave and woke only centuries later. On the road climbing from Tataouine to Chenini, the white Mosque of the Seven Sleepers, with its leaning minaret, stands against an old oratory, a small place of prayer carved into the rock. Beside it, tombs more than 5 meters long spark curiosity: legend says they hold giant saints. On Fridays, women come to light candles: be discreet.

map_keywords: Mosque of the Seven Sleepers Chenini

visits.text: White as far as the eye can see: Chott el-Jérid is the largest salt lake in the Sahara, about 250 km long. A chott is a salt lake that is dry for most of the year. In winter, some flooded areas attract flamingos. The road from Kébili to Tozeur crosses it on a causeway. In summer, scorching air near the ground bends the light, creating mirages that look like stretches of water. Do not walk far out onto the salt crust, which is not always firm.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Tunisia in 9 Days: Djerba, Ksour, the Sahara, and Oases

visits.text: If you could see only one Roman town in Tunisia, choose Dougga. UNESCO, which listed it in 1997, describes it as the best-preserved small Roman town in North Africa. Its Capitol, a temple completed around 166–167 for Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, Rome’s three principal deities, still stands above the forum, the public square. Nearby, the Square of the Winds has a compass rose depicted in its paving. Arrive when the site opens, at 8:30 a.m. in winter, as shade is scarce. Admission costs 8 dinars.

In 168 or 169, the Roman town of Dougga acquired a theater seating 3,500. Climb to the top rows for views over the olive trees surrounding the site and across the plain. After independence, the last residents still living among the ruins were relocated to this plain, to a new village called Nouvelle Dougga. The site became a national archaeological park in 1991.

Damaged by a diplomat, then rebuilt stone by stone, Dougga’s Libyco-Punic Mausoleum has come a long way. This 21 m tomb dates from the 2nd century BC. Its name reflects its blend of two cultures: that of the Libyans, the Berbers of antiquity, and that of Carthage, known as Punic. In 1842, British consul Thomas Reade severely damaged it to remove its inscription, written in both languages and now in the British Museum. Archaeologist Louis Poinssot rebuilt it from 1908 to 1910. Photograph it with the olive trees behind it.

The public latrines at the Baths of the Cyclopes never fail to surprise: in Dougga, as elsewhere in the Roman Empire, people sat side by side without partitions. Excavations here uncovered a mosaic depicting Cyclopes, the one-eyed giants of mythology. A little farther on, the Temple of Juno Caelestis retains a well-preserved sacred enclosure. Signage is sparse: hire a guide or download a map before you come.

days_plan.itin_title: Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem

visits.text: The Sahara Museum in Douz, opened in 1997, tells the story of the region’s nomads, the Mrazig, from whom most residents descend. Displays include a large tent made of wool and dromedary hair, saddles, clothing, and women’s silver jewelry. One room even explains the art of tattooing, used for protection, healing, or adornment. The museum is closed on Mondays. Admission costs 5 dinars, and winter hours are 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m.

activities.text: Walk or ride a dromedary to the Grandes Dunes, at the far end of Douz’s tourist area, where the sand begins. This direct transition from palm grove to desert has earned Douz its nickname, the “gateway to the Sahara.” Agencies in the town center offer rides lasting 1 hour or overnight stays in tents among the dunes. Aim for late afternoon, when the heat eases and the light softens.

If you are in Douz on a Thursday, head to the market: alongside fruit, dates, and bread, donkeys and dromedaries are sold here. On other days, the main square still has its handicraft stalls. From December 19 to 22, 2026, the town hosts the International Festival of the Sahara: four days of dromedary races, poetry readings, and fantasias, charging displays by riders in traditional dress. Book your accommodations well in advance for these dates.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Tunisia in 9 Days: Djerba, Ksour, the Sahara, and Oases

visits.text: Your first striking sight on arriving in El Jem is the enormous amphitheater rising amid a small town on the plain. Built around 238, it stands 36 m tall, the height of a roughly twelve-story building. Between 27,000 and 30,000 spectators could watch the fights here. The large breach in its facade is not the work of time: around 1695, troops of the bey, the ruler of Tunis, opened it to drive out rebels sheltering inside. The site opens as early as 7:30 a.m. in winter: come early, before the heat. Admission costs 12 dinars.

Next, head down into the underground chambers of El Jem’s amphitheater, the most revealing part of the visit. Two galleries intersect at right angles nearly 4 m below the arena. Cells lined them, and openings allowed cages of wild animals to be raised to the arena floor using winches. Since 1985, the amphitheater has hosted an international symphonic music festival every summer: check the program if you are visiting in summer.

The wealthy inhabitants of Thysdrus, the Roman name for El Jem, lived in houses carpeted with mosaics. The El Jem Archaeological Museum displays some beautiful examples, including the procession of Dionysus, the god of wine, or the Muses. The museum also features Villa Africa, a large residence discovered in the 1990s and partly reconstructed, with its wall paintings and a mosaic depicting Africa as a goddess. A combination ticket covers the museum and the amphitheater.

days_plan.itin_title: Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem

visits.text: The Ghriba Synagogue, in the village of Erriadh, is among Africa’s oldest synagogues still in use. According to tradition, Jewish priests are said to have founded this place of worship after the destruction of the First Temple in Jerusalem in 586 BC. The current building dates mainly to the 19th century and 1938: ceramic tiles, carved wood, and stained glass decorate the prayer hall. It is closed on Saturdays for Shabbat. Cover your head and shoulders.

activities.text: An old village with contemporary walls: in 2014, the Djerbahood project turned Erriadh into an open-air street art museum. Around a hundred artists of 30 nationalities painted approximately 250 works on walls made available by residents. The name comes from the words “The Hood,” English for “the neighborhood,” displayed at the village entrance. Erriadh was once called Hara Sghira, Arabic for “the small neighborhood.” Set out early in the morning or late in the day to walk in cooler temperatures.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Tunisia in 9 Days: Djerba, Ksour, the Sahara, and Oases

visits.text: Fifty-four meters: that is the elevation of Djerba’s highest point, where the Guellala Museum stands. The figure shows just how flat the island is. The museum explores the traditions of Djerba and the rest of the country through festivals, legends, pottery, mosaics, and music. It is open daily from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes to explore it.

activities.text: In the hands of Guellala’s potters, the village’s gray clay takes shape on a potter’s wheel with two olivewood disks. For centuries, Guellala has made Djerba’s large jars, which could hold up to 300 liters of grain, dates, or olive oil. There were around 500 potters in the 1950s; only about forty remain. Step into a workshop and ask to see the kilns: a firing takes an average of five days.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Tunisia in 9 Days: Djerba, Ksour, the Sahara, and Oases

visits.text: Hammamet’s medina fits within a square roughly 200 m on each side, its white ramparts standing by the sea. Its walls, completed in the 13th century, were restored in 1727. In the kasbah, the citadel, climb up to the rampart walk, the path along the top of the walls: you’ll see the bay on one side and white rooftops on the other. The painter Paul Klee, who visited in 1914, was struck by the light. In the off-season, the kasbah stays open until around 5:30 p.m.

After the stock market crash of 1929, Romanian billionaire George Sebastian had Dar Sebastian built, a villa 3 km from central Hammamet. In 1943, German general Rommel established his headquarters there. The Tunisian government bought the property in 1962, then added an open-air theater in 1964, where the Hammamet International Festival takes place every summer. Now the International Cultural Center, it is open to visitors: stroll through the garden, then check the festival program if you’re visiting in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem

visits.text: There is no better introduction to Djerba than Borj El Kebir, the square fort that has guarded Houmt Souk’s harbor since the late 14th century. In 1560, off the island, the Ottoman fleet defeated a Christian fleet drawn mainly from Spain, Naples, and Sicily. Dragut, one of the Ottoman commanders, is said to have then had a tower built near the fort from the skulls of the defeated. The bey, the ruler of Tunis, had it demolished in 1848, and an obelisk marks its site. Climb the ramparts for views of the harbor.

A zawiya, or shrine dedicated to a saint, houses part of the Djerba Traditional Heritage Museum in Houmt Souk. This small building from the late 18th century gained a modern wing in 2008. Its galleries showcase clothing and jewelry, pottery, fishing, farming, and festive rituals: everything that sustained island life. Admission costs 8 dinars for nonresidents, and the museum is closed on Fridays.

Spices, silver jewelry, Berber rugs: explore Houmt Souk’s souk by wandering its alleys. At its heart, four covered streets intersect and lead into the jewelers’ souk. Look out for the fondouks, former merchants’ inns built around a courtyard, with shops on the ground floor and a columned gallery upstairs. On Mondays and Thursdays, market days, the town is even livelier. Take your time bargaining; it is customary.

The Mosque of the Turks and the Mosque of the Strangers are the two landmarks of Houmt Souk’s shopping district. The first, built in the 16th century, has Djerba’s only Ottoman-style, or Turkish-style, minaret. The second dates to the 15th century and is recognizable by its large square minaret and domes. Admire them from the street between purchases in the souk.

If you see only one mosque in Djerba, choose Fadhloun Mosque, about ten kilometers southeast of Houmt Souk. Probably built in the 14th century, it belonged to a chain of mosques that formed a second line of defense behind the coastal lookout posts. Around the prayer hall, you will see the Quranic school, two rainwater cisterns, a grain mill, and a bread oven. It is open only in the morning, except on Fridays (5 dinars).

activities.text: Get up early for Houmt Souk’s fish auction, where the day’s catch is sold: it is the only one still held in Djerba. Seated on a high chair, the auctioneer calls out prices in a loud voice. Buyers bid with a nod or just a glance, so watch closely: everything moves very quickly. At the harbor, stacks of earthenware jars are used to catch octopuses, which take shelter inside them.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Tunisia in 9 Days: Djerba, Ksour, the Sahara, and Oases

visits.text: Four hundred fourteen columns of marble, granite, or porphyry (a very hard red rock) support the prayer hall of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. Founded in 670 along with the city, the mosque took on most of its current appearance in 836. Its 31.5 m minaret is described as the oldest still standing in the Muslim world. Non-Muslims can visit the courtyard and view the hall through its doorways. The courtyard is generally open from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m.: come in the morning, with your shoulders and knees covered.

From a distance, they look like two large round swimming pools: these are the Aghlabid Basins, named for the dynasty that ruled the region in the 9th century. Completed in 862, the large basin measures 128 m in diameter, longer than a soccer field. The smaller basin allowed mud to settle before the water flowed into the larger one. The tourist office on the grounds sells the Kairouan combination ticket: climb up to its roof to see the basins from above.

Nicknamed the Mosque of the Barber, the zaouia of Sidi Sahbi, a shrine built around a tomb, houses the grave of Abu Zama al-Balawi, who died in 654 and had been a companion of the Prophet Muhammad. Legend has it that he was buried with three hairs from the Prophet’s beard, hence the nickname. Its corridors and courtyards, expanded in the 17th century, are covered with blue, green, and yellow glazed earthenware tiles from Tunis. Modest attire is required.

Touristy, but intriguing: at the Bir Barouta well in Kairouan, a dromedary still walks in circles to power the mechanism that draws up the water. It is no longer essential, but it keeps an age-old practice alive. A little farther on, the Mosque of the Three Doors, founded in 866, has a facade carved with inscriptions in Kufic, the early Arabic script with angular letters. It can be viewed from outside. You can walk between the two sites through the medina.

If you have another two hours, drive to the Raqqada National Museum of Islamic Art, about ten kilometers southwest of Kairouan. Raqqada served as a residence for the Aghlabid princes starting in 876. Housed since 1986 in a former presidential residence, the museum displays folios from the Blue Quran, a manuscript in Kufic script dating from the 9th and 10th centuries. It is closed on Mondays and closes as early as 4 p.m. in winter and 2 p.m. in summer.

activities.text: Take time to look at Kairouan’s carpets, the city’s great specialty. In the medina, the former governor’s house has become a store where you can watch artisans at work. The demonstration ends with a persistent sales pitch: you are under no obligation to buy. Compare prices in several stores before making a purchase. The house’s terrace also offers a lovely view over the medina at sunset.

The scent of honey and dates wafts around the Aghlabid Basins: it comes from makroudh, Kairouan’s signature pastry. This date-filled semolina cake is dipped in honey. The city is also known for zlabia, another honey-based sweet. Try one on the spot, still warm if possible, then pick up a box for the road.

days_plan.itin_title: Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem

visits.text: Kélibia Fort is worth the climb, especially late in the day, when locals come to sit on the ramparts. Greeks from Sicily founded the town in the late 4th century BC and named it Aspis, “the shield,” because of the shape of the headland. The present fort dates mainly to 1112, built around a Byzantine core from the 6th century. Roman water reservoirs are still visible in the central courtyard. Admission costs 8 dinars, every day.

activities.text: Around 15% of the fish caught in Tunisia passes through the port of Kélibia, amounting to some 15,000 tonnes a year. The town is known for lamparo fishing: at night, powerful lamps attract schools of small fish toward the surface, where they are encircled with a net. Stroll around the port among the trawlers, then go for a swim at La Mansoura Beach, popular with vacationers. In the evening, have grilled fish for dinner near the port.

days_plan.itin_title: Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem

visits.text: There are no standing columns or temples at Kerkouane: here, it’s the bathrooms that surprise visitors. Every house in this Punic, or Carthaginian, city had its own near the entrance, with a sit-down bathtub coated in waterproof red mortar made from crushed pottery. Abandoned around the middle of the 3rd century BC, the city was never rebuilt by the Romans. UNESCO listed it in 1985 as the only Punic city to have survived to the present day. Come before 3 p.m. in winter.

The small Kerkouane Museum, opened in 1987 at the site entrance, helps you imagine the lives of its inhabitants, mainly fishermen and craftspeople. Its best-known piece is a carved wooden sarcophagus lid, called the Lady of Kerkouane, depicting the Phoenician goddess Astarte. Jewelry, including a pendant bearing the symbol of Tanit, the goddess of Carthage, rounds out the visit. The museum is closed on Mondays and closes at 4 p.m. in winter; admission costs 8 dinars.

days_plan.itin_title: Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem

visits.text: About 1,800 years ago, Roman soldiers stood guard at Ksar Ghilane. Tisavar Fort, built no later than the reign of Emperor Commodus (180–192), watched over the Empire’s southern frontier, a line of outposts known as the limes. Its walls, measuring about 30 by 40 meters, rise from the sand an hour’s walk from the oasis. Set out on foot at dawn with water, or ride there on an ATV with a guide.

activities.text: Hot water rises from the ground amid the sand: the spring at Ksar Ghilane fills a pool where you can bathe in warm water year-round. Tamarisk trees shade the oasis paths. Facilities are basic, with a small café and a changing area: this is no spa. Bathe early in the morning or in the late afternoon, once the day trips from Djerba have left.

If you take just one dromedary ride on this trip, make it at Ksar Ghilane. The oasis marks the eastern edge of the Grand Erg Oriental, an immense sea of dunes extending into Algeria. Camel drivers leave the camps in the afternoon to reach the dune crests at sunset. ATVs, available everywhere, are faster but break the silence. Agree on the price and duration before setting out.

It looks as though it could be a thousand years old, yet the Ksar Ghilane palm grove is about seventy years old. It took root in the 1950s, when the first wells allowed nomadic families to settle near the spring. Not far from the oasis, a stele nicknamed the Leclerc Column commemorates the fighting here in 1943, during World War II, by General Leclerc’s troops, who had come from Chad. In the evening, look up: far from any city, the sky fills with stars.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Tunisia in 9 Days: Djerba, Ksour, the Sahara, and Oases

visits.text: On August 10, 1997, the crew of The Phantom Menace, Star Wars Episode I, filmed their final scenes in Tunisia here. Ksar Hadada, a fortified granary from the mid-19th century, 2 km from Ghomrassen, served as the slave quarters of Mos Espa, a city on the planet Tatooine where young Anakin Skywalker grows up. Its narrow lanes lead to a courtyard where stairways seem to lead nowhere. Part of the ksar now hosts overnight guests: ask before entering the courtyards.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Tunisia in 9 Days: Djerba, Ksour, the Sahara, and Oases

visits.text: Many guides describe it as a Star Wars filming location, but Ksar Ouled Soltane needs no cinematic connection. This fortified granary, 24 km south of Tataouine, has 287 ghorfas, vaulted chambers used to store grain, arranged in three to four stories around its courtyards. Restored beginning in 1993, it appears on the 20-dinar banknote issued in 2011. As for the film, its location manager in Tunisia wrote that no filming ever took place here. Come early in the morning or late in the afternoon.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Tunisia in 9 Days: Djerba, Ksour, the Sahara, and Oases

visits.text: Nothing prepares you for the sheer number of mosaics at the Bardo National Museum, home to one of the world’s largest collections of Roman mosaics. Right in the entrance hall, the Triumph of Neptune, found in Sousse, hangs vertically like an enormous painting. Next, look for the 3rd-century Virgil mosaic: the Latin poet sits between two Muses, goddesses of the arts. The museum is closed on Mondays, and admission costs 13 dinars for nonresident visitors.

On September 14, 2023, the Bardo National Museum reopened to the public. It occupies a palace of the beys, the rulers of Tunis during the Ottoman era. The palace shares its grounds with Parliament: during the political crisis of July 2021, both buildings were closed to the public. Don’t miss the Greek bronzes and marble sculptures from the Mahdia shipwreck, an ancient vessel excavated underwater in the early 20th century. Arrive at opening time, 9:30 a.m. in winter and 9 a.m. in summer, and expect a security check.

days_plan.itin_title: Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem

visits.text: Matmata hides its homes underground. Each dwelling is arranged around a large circular pit, 5 to 10 meters deep, with rooms carved into the soft rock opening onto it. Underground, temperatures change little: the rooms stay cool during the day and mildly warm at night, which explains this choice in such a hot climate. The Dar Khadija Museum, open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. (8 dinars in 2025), shows the furnished interior of one of these homes.

For Star Wars fans, this is an essential stop: the Sidi Driss cave dwelling served as Luke Skywalker’s farm on the planet Tatooine. The crew filmed the first movie’s meal scenes here in 1976, then returned in 2000 for Attack of the Clones, Episode II. The site still displays objects and photos from filming, and you can step inside for a drink at the bar. Come early, before the bus tours arrive.

Stone houses, bright blue doors and windows: Tamezret, 10 km from Matmata, is a Berber village perched on a hill where the Berber language is still spoken. Beneath the houses runs a network of tunnels once dug for defense. A small museum run by a local resident showcases jewelry, wedding attire, and Berber traditions, and provides access to these underground passages. Finish at the café at the top, near the mosque, for views of the Matmata Mountains.

activities.text: You can descend into a cave dwelling that is still inhabited: in Matmata, some families open their courtyards to visitors in exchange for a small donation. From the central pit, the layout becomes clear: bedrooms and a kitchen below, with stores of grain, dates, olives, and dried figs on the upper level. In 1969, twenty-two days of rain flooded these homes and caused many to collapse. Most residents nevertheless rebuilt underground.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Tunisia in 9 Days: Djerba, Ksour, the Sahara, and Oases

visits.text: Monty Python filmed scenes from Life of Brian, a movie set in ancient Judea, at the Ribat of Monastir. A ribat is a coastal fort where warrior monks kept watch over the sea. This one was built in 796 by Harthama ibn Ayan, the region’s governor on behalf of the caliph of Baghdad. It is described as the oldest founded by the Arab conquerors in the Maghreb. Climb the watchtower for views of the city and beach. Admission is 8 dinars, and it is open daily.

The golden dome of Habib Bourguiba’s mausoleum gleams at the end of a 200 m walkway in Monastir’s Sidi El Mézeri Cemetery. The father of Tunisian independence, who died in 2000, commissioned it during his lifetime, with construction beginning in 1963. Two 25 m minarets flank the building. A small museum displays his desk from the Carthage Palace, his pens, glasses, and passports. Admission is free, but hours vary: check locally.

days_plan.itin_title: Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem

visits.text: A green basin suddenly opens up in the middle of the city: this is the Corbeille de Nefta, a natural hollow with rocky walls, filled with palm trees. It was once fed by 152 springs. Most have dried up, and many palm trees disappeared in the early 1980s. Domes around it mark the shrines of the city’s saints. Come in the late afternoon, when the light is softest.

Nearly a hundred marabouts, small domed tombs of saints, are scattered throughout Nefta. The most revered saint, Sidi Bou Ali, came from Morocco in the 13th century and made the city a center of Sufism, the mystical branch of Islam. He also established an annual pilgrimage centered on his zaouia, or shrine. Stroll through the Ouled Cherif and El Bayadha neighborhoods, with their ocher brick houses and covered passageways. Dress modestly near the shrines, which remain places of prayer.

activities.text: You will end the day in Nefta’s palm grove, which covers more than 1,600 hectares. It can be visited on foot or by horse-drawn carriage, offering a chance to see how water flows from garden to garden through irrigation channels. As in Tozeur, deglet nour is the main variety grown here. Avoid driving at night: France Diplomatie advises against nighttime driving away from major roads.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Tunisia in 9 Days: Djerba, Ksour, the Sahara, and Oases

places.name: Sidi Bou Said

visits.text: Sailors called him “the master of the seas” because they believed he was their protector: Abou Saïd el-Béji, a saint who died in 1231, had retired to this hill. The village of Sidi Bou Saïd bears his name. It overlooks the Gulf of Tunis from a 130 m cliff. It has been protected since 1915: white walls and blue doors are the rule here. Walk up the main street to Café des Nattes and order mint tea with pine nuts.

The village’s most beautiful house is open to visitors: Dar Ennejma Ezzahra, “the shining star,” Baron Rodolphe d’Erlanger’s palace in Sidi Bou Saïd. The painter, who died in 1932, was also a musicologist, a specialist in the study of music. He was responsible for securing the village’s protection. Now home to the Center for Arab and Mediterranean Music, the palace displays a collection of historic instruments and hosts concerts. Hours vary: check the center’s website before heading up.

activities.text: Then head down to Café des Délices in Sidi Bou Saïd to end the day. Opened in the late 1960s, it clings to the cliff overlooking the Gulf of Tunis, with Carthage in the distance. Singer Patrick Bruel dedicated a song to it in 1999, “Au café des Délices.” Arrive an hour before sunset to find a seat on the terrace.

Cafe des Delices Sidi Bou Said

visits.text: Climb the stairs of the tower at the Ribat of Sousse: from the top, you can look down into the fort’s courtyard and over the medina’s rooftops. A ribat was a fort where warrior monks lived and kept watch over the coast. Built around 775, this one was completely rebuilt in 821 by the emir, or prince, Ziyadat Allah I. It has been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site along with the medina since 1988. Admission costs 8 dinars, and the site is open daily.

There is no large minaret at the Great Mosque of Sousse: the neighboring ribat’s tower was used for the call to prayer. Built in 850–851 by Emir Abu al-Abbas, the mosque looks more like a fortress than a place of prayer. You can visit its courtyard for an admission fee, wearing clothing that covers your shoulders and knees, while the prayer hall is reserved for worshippers. Avoid the Friday noon prayer.

Allow at least one hour for the Sousse Archaeological Museum, housed in the kasbah, the 9th-century citadel overlooking the medina. Its mosaic collection is Tunisia’s second largest after the Bardo’s. Most come from Hadrumetum, Roman Sousse. Two of the Bardo’s most famous mosaics, the Triumph of Neptune and Virgil, also come from Sousse. Finish in the garden, with its views over the medina and harbor. The museum is closed on Mondays; admission costs 10 dinars.

activities.text: If you stay until late in the day, walk around the 2.5 km ramparts of the Sousse medina. They were built in 859, when the Aghlabid dynasty ruled the region. Enter through Bab el Gharbi, the western gate, then head down the shopping lanes toward the ribat as the evening light turns the stone golden.

places.name: Tataouine

visits.text: Dinosaurs once lived here: the rocks around Tataouine date from the Cretaceous, a period that ended 66 million years ago. Several important fossils have been unearthed here. The small Mémoire de la Terre museum, on the road to Chenini 2.5 km from the center, displays these fossils, meteorites that fell in the region, and dinosaur reconstructions. A large dinosaur statue marks its location on the hill. Check opening hours before you go.

activities.text: In Berber, Tataouine means “the springs,” and its name inspired Tatooine, the desert planet in Star Wars. Life in the city revolves around its souk, which opened in 1892 with more than a hundred shops. Try a gazelle horn, Tataouine’s specialty: a crescent-shaped pastry filled with almond paste. The market takes place twice a week, including Mondays, when the city is much livelier.

visits.text: Here, time runs backward: on the minaret of the Great Mosque of Testour, the clock’s hands turn in reverse. The present-day town was built around 1609 by Moriscos, Muslims expelled from Spain. Why backward? The most widespread explanation is nostalgia: turning back time toward a lost Andalusia. After standing still for nearly three centuries, the clock was restarted on November 11, 2014. Look up from the central square.

activities.text: Then stroll through Testour’s streets, laid out in a grid like those of southern Spanish towns. Since 1967, the town has hosted an international festival of malouf, a form of Arab-Andalusian music. Sit at an outdoor café on the central square for a coffee before heading to Dougga, about a 40-minute drive away.

activities.text: If you enjoy hilltop villages, stop in Toujane on the road to Matmata. The old village, almost empty now that most residents live farther down in Toujane Nouvelle, spreads in tiers along the edge of a valley, with walled homes and arched doorways. A rocky path climbs to the ksar at the top, with sweeping views of the Dahar Mountains, the mountain range in southeastern Tunisia. Watch your step: open shafts reveal former homes dug into the ground.

visits.text: To us, the Ouled el-Hadef quarter offers the finest lesson in architecture in southern Tunisia. In this old part of Tozeur, whose oldest sections date to the 14th century, the facades are made of pale clay bricks. Masons set some bricks slightly forward to create diamonds and chevrons, patterns inspired by carpets and Arabic script. Wander through the covered passageways in the late afternoon, when the low sun brings out the relief patterns.

Tunisia’s first private museum, Dar Cheraït opened in Tozeur in 1990 at the initiative of Abderrazak Cheraït. Its rooms recreate 19th-century Tunisian life through jewelry, pottery, and interiors. You can also see the water-sharing system devised by Ibn Chabbat, a scholar born in Tozeur in 1221. Each garden received water in turn through small channels called seguias, with the duration measured by a water clock. Allow 1 hour for your visit.

Eden Palm, less than a kilometer from central Tozeur, is an open-air museum devoted to the date palm. Information panels and a palm garden explain the tree, the diversity of dates, and life in the oasis. Artisans demonstrate how they turn palm leaves and wood into objects. The sharecropper’s hut introduces the work done throughout the year by a farmer who cultivates someone else’s land. From October to December, tastings are available by reservation.

Kitschy but surprising, Chak Wak park in Tozeur’s palm grove traces the history of Earth and humanity across five hectares, from dinosaurs to the major religions. Its name comes from an imaginary island in One Thousand and One Nights. Created by the founder of the Dar Cheraït Museum, it even includes a model of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. It is a fun stop with children, best visited during the cooler hours.

activities.text: Explore Tozeur’s palm grove by horse-drawn carriage or on foot, beneath some 400,000 palms spread across nearly 1,000 hectares. The main variety grown here is deglet nour, the “date of light,” harvested in November. In the past, 150 to 200 springs watered the gardens. Modern wells have dried up many of them, and today the water comes mainly from the deep aquifer, an underground water reserve. Sample fresh dates from a grower.

If you are flying home, Tozeur–Nefta International Airport is about 3 km north of Tozeur. Transavia connects it to Paris-Orly year-round, and Tunisair Express operates flights to Tunis, mainly in winter. Flights are limited, so book them before finalizing the rest of your trip. Otherwise, allow a long day of driving to return to Djerba.

visits.text: Cars stay outside: beyond Bab el Bhar, Tunis’s medina is explored on foot. The gate’s name means “Gate of the Sea.” It once provided access to Christian merchants’ warehouses. Beyond it lies the old Arab city, founded in 698 around Zitouna Mosque. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. Map apps quickly lose their way here: use Rue Jamaa Zitouna, the shopping street leading to the Great Mosque, to get your bearings.

Although open only to Muslims, Zitouna Mosque remains the heart of Tunis’s medina. Rebuilt in 864, it long housed a major Islamic university. In 1958, President Bourguiba moved its courses to a faculty of theology. Its 43 m minaret dates only to 1894. Souks, or covered markets, crowd around it, including the perfumers’ Souk El Attarine, built in the early 18th century. Ask to smell the essences before buying, and confirm the price per bottle.

The medina’s finest purchase fits in one hand: a chechia from Souk Ech-Chaouachine. This round felted-wool cap, often red, is the traditional headwear of Tunisian men. Its makers form one of the country’s oldest guilds, or trade associations. This covered souk has been dedicated to them since the 17th century. Step into a shop, compare the shades, and try several sizes before choosing.

In 1631, an oratory, a small prayer room in Tunis’s medina, became Youssef Dey Mosque. It stands near Kasbah Square. On the square is Dar El Bey, a late-18th-century palace that now houses the Office of the Head of Government. Hammouda Pacha Mosque, built in 1655, completes the walk. View these buildings from outside, as Tunis’s mosques are reserved for worshippers. In front of government buildings, put your camera away and keep your distance from police officers on guard.

White domes cluster together, like those on Istanbul’s mosques: this is Sidi Mahrez Mosque, on Bab Souika Square. Built from 1692 to 1697 on the model of the great Ottoman mosques, it has no minaret. Its domes even appear on the emblem of the city of Tunis. The monument is reserved for worshippers, but the square offers a good view. Opposite stands the Zaouia of Sidi Mahrez, the shrine of the medina’s patron saint: wear clothing that covers your body if you approach the entrance.

If an exhibition is on, step inside Kheireddine Palace, in the heart of Tunis’s medina. The reformist minister Kheireddine Pacha had it built between 1860 and 1870, combining the layout of a Tunisian house with Italian-style interior decoration. It became the Tunis City Museum in 1999 and hosts exhibitions by Tunisian and international artists, including the annual exhibition of the Union of Tunisian Visual Artists (painters, sculptors, and photographers). The program changes often: check it on-site.

After the narrow lanes, step into another era: Avenue Habib Bourguiba is lined with Art Nouveau and Art Deco facades, cafés, and shops. St. Vincent de Paul Cathedral, built from 1893 to 1897 in a style inspired by Romanesque and Byzantine churches, faces the French Embassy. The Municipal Theater, inaugurated in 1902, has a sculpted facade. A statue honors Ibn Khaldun, a 14th-century thinker born in Tunis. If a crowd gathers, move away, as recommended by the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs.

activities.text: Finish at Tunis’s Central Market, a covered market hall built in 1891 at the intersection of Rue Charles-de-Gaulle, Rue d’Allemagne, and Rue d’Espagne. Residents shop among the fresh produce stalls, away from the tourist stores. This is the place to taste local dates or olives. Come in the morning, when the market is liveliest, and keep some small change handy to buy goods by weight.

The drive from Kerkouane to Tunis, where the loop ends, takes about 2 hours. Plan to arrive before nightfall: the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs strongly advises against driving at night in Tunisia. If you’re returning the car at Tunis-Carthage Airport, allow extra time to refuel and have the car inspected before your flight.

days_plan.itin_title: Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem
Tunisia in 8 Days: Carthage, Dougga, Kairouan, and El Jem

visits.text: The water for Carthage’s fountains began its journey here: on the mountain south of Zaghouan, the Temple of the Waters marks the source of the Roman aqueduct. This nymphaeum, a monumental fountain shaped like a temple, is bordered by a semicircular portico with niches that once held statues. From here, the water reached Carthage along a main route just over 90 km long, built in the 2nd century. Allow 45 minutes on site.

activities.text: In Zaghouan, cakes are flavored with nesri, the local name for blossom water made from the dog rose, a wild rose. Andalusians, Muslims expelled from Spain, introduced its cultivation here. It is used in kaak warka, a regional pastry, among other specialties. In the old town, look for the Roman arch, a remnant of the ancient city of Ziqua. Buy a bottle of dog rose blossom water or a box of kaak warka before getting back on the road.
